passage.sceneTitle: The Mole Comes Up into the Spring
passage.preamble: Mole is a small animal who lives by himself in a little house underground. He has spent the whole morning cleaning it from top to bottom.

numberedLines.text: The Mole had been working very hard all the morning, spring-cleaning his little home.
First with brooms, then with dusters; then on ladders and steps and chairs, with a brush
and a pail of whitewash; till he had dust in his throat and eyes, and splashes of
whitewash all over his black fur, and an aching back and weary arms. Spring was moving
in the air above and in the earth below and around him, penetrating even his dark and
lowly little house with its spirit of divine discontent and longing. It was small
wonder, then, that he suddenly flung down his brush on the floor, said “Bother!” and “O
blow!” and also “Hang spring-cleaning!” and bolted out of the house without even waiting
to put on his coat. Something up above was calling him imperiously, and he made for the
steep little tunnel which answered in his case to the gravelled carriage-drive owned by
animals whose residences are nearer to the sun and air. So he scraped and scratched and
scrabbled and scrooged and then he scrooged again and scrabbled and scratched and
scraped, working busily with his little paws and muttering to himself, “Up we go! Up we
go!” till at last, pop! his snout came out into the sunlight, and he found himself
rolling in the warm grass of a great meadow.
“This is fine!” he said to himself. “This is better than whitewashing!” The sunshine
struck hot on his fur, soft breezes caressed his heated brow, and after the seclusion of
the cellarage he had lived in so long the carol of happy birds fell on his dulled
hearing almost like a shout. Jumping off all his four legs at once, in the joy of living
and the delight of spring without its cleaning, he pursued his way across the meadow
till he reached the hedge on the further side.
“Hold up!” said an elderly rabbit at the gap. “Sixpence for the privilege of passing by
the private road!” He was bowled over in an instant by the impatient and contemptuous
Mole, who trotted along the side of the hedge chaffing the other rabbits as they peeped
hurriedly from their holes to see what the row was about. “Onion-sauce! Onion-sauce!” he
remarked jeeringly, and was gone before they could think of a thoroughly satisfactory
reply.
He thought his happiness was complete when, as he meandered aimlessly along, suddenly he
stood by the edge of a full-fed river. Never in his life had he seen a river before—this
sleek, sinuous, full-bodied animal, chasing and chuckling, gripping things with a gurgle
and leaving them with a laugh, to fling itself on fresh playmates that shook themselves
free, and were caught and held again. All was a-shake and a-shiver—glints and gleams and
sparkles, rustle and swirl, chatter and bubble. The Mole was bewitched, entranced,
fascinated. By the side of the river he trotted as one trots, when very small, by the
side of a man who holds one spell-bound by exciting stories; and when tired at last, he
sat on the bank, while the river still chattered on to him, a babbling procession of the
best stories in the world, sent from the heart of the earth to be told at last to the
insatiable sea.
As he sat on the grass and looked across the river, a dark hole in the bank opposite,
just above the water’s edge, caught his eye, and dreamily he fell to considering what a
nice snug dwelling-place it would make for an animal with few wants and fond of a bijou
riverside residence, above flood level and remote from noise and dust. As he gazed,
something bright and small seemed to twinkle down in the heart of it, vanished, then
twinkled once more like a tiny star. But it could hardly be a star in such an unlikely
situation; and it was too glittering and small for a glow-worm. Then, as he looked, it
winked at him, and so declared itself to be an eye; and a small face began gradually to
grow up round it, like a frame round a picture.
A brown little face, with whiskers.
A grave round face, with the same twinkle in its eye that had first attracted his
notice.
Small neat ears and thick silky hair.
It was the Water Rat!
Then the two animals stood and regarded each other cautiously.
“Hullo, Mole!” said the Water Rat.
“Hullo, Rat!” said the Mole.
“Would you like to come over?” enquired the Rat presently.
“Oh, it’s all very well to talk,” said the Mole, rather pettishly, he being new to a
river and riverside life and its ways.
The Rat said nothing, but stooped and unfastened a rope and hauled on it; then lightly
stepped into a little boat which the Mole had not observed. It was painted blue outside
and white within, and was just the size for two animals; and the Mole’s whole heart went
out to it at once, even though he did not yet fully understand its uses.
The Rat sculled smartly across and made fast. Then he held up his forepaw as the Mole
stepped gingerly down. “Lean on that!” he said. “Now then, step lively!” and the Mole to
his surprise and rapture found himself actually seated in the stern of a real boat.
“This has been a wonderful day!” said he, as the Rat shoved off and took to the sculls
again. “Do you know, I’ve never been in a boat before in all my life.”

stem.text: Read lines 1 to 4. What had the Mole been doing all morning?

rows.key: Cleaning his little home from top to bottom.

options.value: Digging out a brand new tunnel.
options.tagChildHint: A true fact from somewhere else does not answer this question. Find the part the question points to.
options.execution: Lines 9 to 13 have him scraping up a tunnel that already exists, not digging a new one, and they sit outside the window the stem names.

options.value: Cleaning his little home from top to bottom.
Painting his house blue outside and white inside.
options.tagChildHint: Two people are being described. Check which one each detail belongs to.
options.execution: Blue outside and white within is the Rat's boat at line 60; the colours are carried across to the house.

options.value: Resting his aching back and weary arms.
options.tagChildHint: Being in the lines is not enough. Check it answers the question you were asked.
options.execution: Line 4 gives 'an aching back and weary arms' as what the morning left him with. The phrase is true and inside the window; resting is the wrong element of it.

options.value: Singing along with the happy birds.
options.tagChildHint: A true fact from somewhere else does not answer this question. Find the part the question points to.
options.execution: The birds sing at line 18 and the Mole never sings anywhere. A morning of work with birds outside invites it and nothing states it.

rows.hintCore: The very first line names the morning. Start there.
rows.walkScript: Go straight to line 1. It tells you the Mole had been spring-cleaning his little home. That gives you your answer. The other choices happen later in the passage.

stem.text: Read lines 3 to 4. What was all over the Mole's black fur?

options.value: Dust, which had got into his throat and eyes.
options.tagChildHint: Being in the lines is not enough. Check it answers the question you were asked.
options.execution: Line 3 puts the dust in his throat and eyes. True, inside the window, and the wrong element for a question about his fur.

options.value: Bits of straw from his brooms.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: Straw appears nowhere in the passage; the brooms at line 2 make it sound like a detail that ought to be there.

options.value: Warm grass from the great meadow.
options.tagChildHint: A true fact from somewhere else does not answer this question. Find the part the question points to.
options.execution: The warm grass is line 15, after he comes up into the meadow — a true detail from a different part of the passage.

options.value: Splashes of whitewash.
Blue and white paint.
options.tagChildHint: Two people are being described. Check which one each detail belongs to.
options.execution: Blue and white are the boat's colours at line 60, transferred onto the fur.

rows.hintCore: One thing is in his eyes, one thing is on his fur. Which does the question want?
rows.walkScript: Line 3 has the dust in his throat and eyes. Line 4 puts the whitewash 'all over his black fur'. So it is splashes of whitewash; the grass and the paint come later.

stem.text: Read lines 5 to 9. Why did the Mole suddenly stop cleaning and run outside?

rows.key: Spring outside was pulling at him and he could not sit still.

options.value: He had finished every job in the house.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: Nothing says the work was finished; line 7 has him fling the brush down in the middle of it.

options.value: Spring outside was pulling at him and he could not sit still.
His back and arms hurt too much to go on.
options.tagChildHint: A racing heart usually shows a feeling. Check what the character is feeling right then.
options.execution: Line 4 gives the aching back and weary arms — a physical state offered in place of the pull of spring at lines 5 and 6.

options.value: The Water Rat called him from up above.
options.tagChildHint: Ask what exactly made this happen. Re-read the moment step by step.
options.execution: The Water Rat does not appear until line 54. Line 9 says 'something up above was calling him', and this hands that to a character.

options.value: He wanted to find the river he had heard about.
options.tagChildHint: A reason has to be given, not guessed. Ask what the text says about why.
options.execution: He has not heard of the river — line 29 says he had never seen one in his life. The motive is supplied by the reader.

rows.hintCore: Read the sentence that comes just before he throws the brush down.
rows.walkScript: Line 5 puts spring 'in the air above and in the earth below'. Line 6 has it reach even his 'lowly little house'. Line 7 has him fling the brush down. That pull sends him out, and the Rat has not appeared yet.

stem.text: Read line 18. What does 'the carol of happy birds' mean?

options.value: A Christmas song the birds had learned.
options.tagChildHint: You know one meaning for this word. Check that meaning fits what the sentence is saying here.
options.execution: The Christmas sense of 'carol' is the one a child meets first, and the passage supplies no season but spring to argue against it. NOTE REPAIRED 2026-08-16 (delivery 52): this is the DOMINANT sense arriving ahead of the passage's, not a second sense being matched to the wrong one. The tag is grandfathered; the description of the error is not.

options.value: The singing of the birds.
A church bell ringing far away.
options.tagChildHint: That meaning belongs to a different word. Read the sentence again.
options.execution: A bell is nowhere in the passage; it arrives with the Christmas sense and nothing else.

options.value: The sound of the river chattering.
options.tagChildHint: A true fact from somewhere else does not answer this question. Find the part the question points to.
options.execution: The river chatters at line 36, much later — a true sound from a different part.

options.value: A shout from someone in the meadow.
options.tagChildHint: Figures of speech are not facts. Ask what the words are really saying.
options.execution: Line 19 says the singing fell 'almost like a shout'. This takes the comparison as the thing itself.

rows.hintCore: Whose carol is it? Read the three words straight after it.
rows.walkScript: Read the words after 'carol' in line 18. They are 'of happy birds'. A carol is a song, so the birds are singing. Christmas is the word's other sense.

stem.text: Read lines 23 to 27. What does the way the Mole treats the rabbits show about him?

rows.key: He is so excited that he will not stop for anyone.

options.value: He is frightened of the older rabbit.
options.tagChildHint: Pick the word you can prove from the text. Close is not the same.
options.execution: Fear is an approximation of the two words the passage does give — 'impatient and contemptuous' at line 23.

options.value: He is so excited that he will not stop for anyone.
He is a cruel animal who is always unkind.
options.tagChildHint: Does the passage really go that far? Check the strongest word in the option.
options.execution: 'Always unkind' pushes one rush past a hedge into a permanent character.

options.value: He is rushing home to get his dinner.
options.tagChildHint: A reason has to be given, not guessed. Ask what the text says about why.
options.execution: Dinner is nowhere in the passage, and he is going away from his house rather than towards it.

options.value: He is sorry at once for knocking the rabbit over.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: Line 26 has him 'gone before they could think of a reply', which leaves no room for the remorse this asserts.

rows.hintCore: He is not thinking about the rabbits at all. What is he thinking about?
rows.walkScript: Line 23 gives two words: 'impatient and contemptuous'. That word 'contemptuous' means looking down on someone. So he will not stop for anyone. It happens in one rush past the hedge.
